prompt: A model counts failures among a fixed set of disks over one year. Which assumptions make that count binomial?

options.text: Continue adding disks until the first failure.
options.explanation: That changes the stopping rule to a waiting-time problem.

options.text: All disks share a failure-inducing power supply.
options.explanation: A shared cause can make their outcomes dependent.

options.text: Independent disk outcomes with the same failure probability.
options.explanation: A fixed number of equal-probability independent yes/no trials defines the binomial model.

options.text: Only that the average failure rate is known.
options.explanation: An average alone does not establish independence or identical probabilities.

workedExample: Identify one trial per original disk and one yes/no outcome over the specified year. Then check the fixed population, common probability and independence. Replacement disks would create additional trials outside this population.

prompt: For five independent fair coin flips, why is the probability of exactly three heads larger than the probability of the particular sequence heads-heads-heads-tails-tails?

options.text: The final tails do not count as part of the experiment.
options.explanation: All five outcomes are required to specify the sequence.

options.text: Several distinct sequences contain exactly three heads.
options.explanation: The count event combines all those equally likely sequences.

options.text: The coin becomes biased after three heads.
options.explanation: The model states independent fair flips.

options.text: Head counts are all equally likely.
options.explanation: Counts aggregate different numbers of sequences.

workedExample: A particular sequence fixes the positions of every head and tail. A head-count event leaves those positions free, so it includes several sequences. The binomial coefficient accounts for those arrangements.

prompt: A link loses each packet independently with a fixed nonzero probability below one. If a transfer uses more packets, what happens to the chance it loses none?

options.text: It decreases because every additional packet must also survive.
options.explanation: All-survive probability multiplies another factor below one.

options.text: It stays equal to one packet’s survival probability.
options.explanation: That ignores the need for every packet to survive.

options.text: It becomes zero as soon as expected losses reach one.
options.explanation: An expected count is not a guaranteed count.

options.text: It increases because more packets average away losses.
options.explanation: Averaging does not repair a requirement that no packet be lost.

workedExample: Write the success event as all packets surviving. Adding a packet imposes another condition. The complement gives at least one loss, which becomes more likely as the fixed-probability independent exposure grows.
